claim: 3-chloropiperidines (3-CePs) are a novel class of candidate anticancer agents developed to improve the pharmacological profile of nitrogen mustard-based chemotherapeutics.
source: Studies from our group highlighted 3-chloropiperidines (3-CePs) as a novel class of candidate anticancer agents developed to improve the pharmacological profile of nitrogen mustard-based chemotherapeutics, characterized by a fast and affordable synthesis (Carraro et al., 2021; Carraro et al., 2019; Helbing et al., 2020; Sosic et al., 2017; Zuravka et al., 2015a; Zuravka et al., 2014; Zuravka et al., 2015b).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior work from the authors' group describing the development and characterization of 3-CePs.

claim: 3-chloropiperidines are characterized by a fast and affordable synthesis.
source: Studies from our group highlighted 3-chloropiperidines (3-CePs) as a novel class of candidate anticancer agents developed to improve the pharmacological profile of nitrogen mustard-based chemotherapeutics, characterized by a fast and affordable synthesis (Carraro et al., 2021; Carraro et al., 2019; Helbing et al., 2020; Sosic et al., 2017; Zuravka et al., 2015a; Zuravka et al., 2014; Zuravka et al., 2015b).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work describing the synthesis of 3-CePs.

claim: 3-chloropiperidines induce DNA lesions, which is conceivably responsible for their cytotoxicity on tested cancer cell lines.
source: As intended, these agents were demonstrated to induce DNA lesions, a mechanism conceivably responsible for their cytotoxicity on tested cancer cell lines (Carraro et al., 2021; Carraro et al., 2019; Helbing et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work demonstrating DNA lesion induction by 3-CePs.

claim: A subset of 3-CeP derivatives showed preferential activity against pancreatic adenocarcinoma (PAAD) BxPC-3 cells in 2D and 3D cell culture compared to treatment-resistant cell lines like HCT-15 from colorectal cancer.
source: Interestingly, despite their expected broad-acting MoA, a subset of derivatives showed preferential activity against pancreatic adenocarcinoma (PAAD)BxPC-3 cells in 2D and 3D cell culture when compared to other treatment-resistant cell lines (e.g. HCT-15 from colorectal cancer).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work showing differential activity of 3-CePs across cell lines.

claim: The 72 hr IC50 ratio of HCT-15 to BxPC-3 is 50 for compound M and 10 for compound B.
source: From this premise, the two compounds were chosen along with the highly sensitive BxPC-3 cell line and the low-sensitive HCT-15 colorectal adenocarcinoma cell line (72 hr IC50 HCT-15/IC50 BxPC-3: 50 for M, 10 for B) (Carraro et al., 2019; Helbing et al., 2020)
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work reporting IC50 values for compounds M and B.

claim: BxPC-3 and HCT-15 cells showed very comparable DNA damage accumulation after 6 hr treatment with both compounds M and B.
source: Surprisingly, the two cell lines showed very comparable DNA damage accumulation, in both cases higher after treatment with M compared to B (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B measuring DNA single-strand breaks.

claim: DNA damage accumulation was higher after treatment with M compared to B in both BxPC-3 and HCT-15 cells.
source: Surprisingly, the two cell lines showed very comparable DNA damage accumulation, in both cases higher after treatment with M compared to B (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Compound M induced a persisting block in G1 throughout the observation time in BxPC-3 cells.
source: While M induced a persisting block in G1 throughout the observation time in BxPC-3 cells, this block was absent in HCT-15 cells.
evidence: Supported by cell cycle distribution analysis data shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The G1 block induced by compound M was absent in HCT-15 cells.
source: While M induced a persisting block in G1 throughout the observation time in BxPC-3 cells, this block was absent in HCT-15 cells.
evidence: Supported by cell cycle distribution analysis data shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Compound B induced an early G2/S block in HCT-15 cells at 6 hr, which was not observed at later time points.
source: In contrast, B induced an early G2/S block in HCT-15 cells (6 hr), which was not observed at later time points, while such a block was most obvious at 12 hr for BxPC-3 cells.
evidence: Supported by cell cycle distribution analysis data shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Compound B induced a G2/S block most obvious at 12 hr in BxPC-3 cells.
source: In contrast, B induced an early G2/S block in HCT-15 cells (6 hr), which was not observed at later time points, while such a block was most obvious at 12 hr for BxPC-3 cells.
evidence: Supported by cell cycle distribution analysis data shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Only HCT-15 cells showed an increase in the γH2AX-positive population after treatment with 3-CePs, despite comparable DNA damage accumulation in both cell lines.
source: Interestingly, despite the comparable DNA damage accumulation in the two cell lines, only HCT-15 showed an increase in the γH2AX-positive population, suggesting a more efficient engagement of the DNA repair machinery.
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1D measuring H2AX phosphorylation.

claim: The increase in γH2AX-positive population in HCT-15 cells suggests a more efficient engagement of the DNA repair machinery.
source: Interestingly, despite the comparable DNA damage accumulation in the two cell lines, only HCT-15 showed an increase in the γH2AX-positive population, suggesting a more efficient engagement of the DNA repair machinery.
evidence: Based on inference from the observed γH2AX phosphorylation data and established knowledge that γH2AX is a marker of DNA repair activation.

claim: Cell-specific mechanisms after the first event of DNA damage are responsible for the different sensitivity to 3-CePs.
source: Taken together, these results indicated that cell-specific mechanisms after the first event of DNA damage are responsible for the different sensitivity to 3-CePs.
evidence: Based on inference from the combined observations of comparable DNA damage but different downstream responses (cell cycle, DNA repair activation).

claim: RNA-seq was performed on total RNA of HCT-15 and BxPC-3 cells exposed to DMSO 0.5% (control) or treated with M (10 nM) or B (200 nM) for 6 hr and 12 hr.
source: RNA-seq was performed on total RNA of HCT-15 and BxPC-3 cells exposed to DMSO 0.5% (control) or treated with M (10 nM) or B (200 nM) for 6 hr and 12 hr (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A) as in previous experiments.
evidence: Describes the experimental design for RNA-seq data collection.

claim: Principal component analysis of all transcripts separated samples within each cell line according to treatment and time point.
source: Principal component analysis (PCA) of all transcripts separated samples within each cell line according to treatment and time point (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), suggesting a clear transcriptional reprogramming after treatment.
evidence: Supported by PCA analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The expression of a large number of genes changed significantly in both cell lines after exposure to 3-CePs.
source: In fact, differential expression (DE) analysis showed that the expression of a large number of genes changed significantly in both cell lines after exposure to 3-CePs (p<0.05, independent hypothesis weighting [IHW] multiple testing correction) (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C), especially at 6 hr in BxPC-3 cells and upon treatment with B in HCT-15 cells.
evidence: Supported by differential expression analysis data shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Gene expression changes were especially prominent at 6 hr in BxPC-3 cells and upon treatment with B in HCT-15 cells.
source: In fact, differential expression (DE) analysis showed that the expression of a large number of genes changed significantly in both cell lines after exposure to 3-CePs (p<0.05, independent hypothesis weighting [IHW] multiple testing correction) (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C), especially at 6 hr in BxPC-3 cells and upon treatment with B in HCT-15 cells.
evidence: Supported by differential expression analysis data shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: A strong translational response was identified in BxPC-3 cells after treatment.
source: Unexpectedly, we identified a strong translational response in BxPC-3 cells after treatment, a process which is typically attenuated in stress conditions, as was the exposure to our DNA damaging agents, to allow proper recovery of the protein quality control machinery (Burger et al., 2010; Shenton et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by gene ontology enrichment analysis of differential expression data, with citations to prior work on translational responses to stress.

claim: Translation is typically attenuated in stress conditions to allow proper recovery of the protein quality control machinery.
source: Unexpectedly, we identified a strong translational response in BxPC-3 cells after treatment, a process which is typically attenuated in stress conditions, as was the exposure to our DNA damaging agents, to allow proper recovery of the protein quality control machinery (Burger et al., 2010; Shenton et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work on cellular stress responses.

claim: A strong regulation of genes mediating protein stability and catabolism was observed in HCT-15 cells.
source: In contrast, a strong regulation of genes mediating protein stability and catabolism was observed in the low-sensitive cell line.
evidence: Supported by gene ontology enrichment analysis of differential expression data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: HCT-15 cells activated genes involved in the DNA damage response.
source: In addition, HCT-15 cells activated genes involved in the DDR, consistent with their higher ability to detect and respond to DSBs.
evidence: Supported by gene ontology enrichment analysis of differential expression data, consistent with prior observations of γH2AX phosphorylation.

claim: The activation of DNA damage response genes in HCT-15 cells is consistent with their higher ability to detect and respond to double-strand breaks.
source: In addition, HCT-15 cells activated genes involved in the DDR, consistent with their higher ability to detect and respond to DSBs.
evidence: Based on inference connecting transcriptional data with prior observations of γH2AX phosphorylation.

claim: Both DNA repair and proteostasis mechanisms point toward the activation of an adaptive stress response in the low-sensitive cell line.
source: Both these two mechanisms pointed toward the activation of an adaptive stress response in the low-sensitive cell line.
evidence: Based on inference from the combined observations of DNA repair and proteostasis gene activation in HCT-15 cells.

claim: Genes involved in ribosome biogenesis and DNA repair were upregulated particularly after 6 hr of treatment in BxPC-3 cells.
source: Genes involved in ribosome biogenesis and DNA repair turned out to be upregulated, particularly after 6 hr of treatment in BxPC-3 cells (Clusters 2 and 3, Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by clustering and functional enrichment analysis of differential expression data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Silencing of pro-survival genes involved in microtubule organization and the JAK-STAT cascade was detected at 6 hr in BxPC-3 cells.
source: Besides, silencing of pro-survival genes involved in microtubule organization and the JAK-STAT cascade (Cluster 1, Figure 2D) was detected at the same time point.
evidence: Supported by clustering and functional enrichment analysis of differential expression data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: BxPC-3 cells boosted carbohydrate metabolism only after 12 hr of treatment, most likely an attempt to recover in extremis.
source: Only after 12 hr of treatment (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A), BxPC-3 cells boosted carbohydrate metabolism, most likely an attempt to recover in extremis (Lin et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by clustering and functional enrichment analysis of differential expression data, with citation to prior work and speculation about biological interpretation.

claim: HCT-15 cells upregulated clusters of genes mediating DNA repair, protein stability, and mitochondrial activity as early as 6 hr of treatment.
source: Also, HCT-15 cells upregulated clusters of genes mediating DNA repair, protein stability, and mitochondrial activity as early as 6 hr of treatment, suggesting this time point as the most informative to describe the response to 3-CePs (Clusters 4 and 6, Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by clustering and functional enrichment analysis of differential expression data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The 6 hr time point is the most informative to describe the response to 3-CePs in HCT-15 cells.
source: Also, HCT-15 cells upregulated clusters of genes mediating DNA repair, protein stability, and mitochondrial activity as early as 6 hr of treatment, suggesting this time point as the most informative to describe the response to 3-CePs (Clusters 4 and 6, Figure 2D).
evidence: Based on inference from the observation that key response pathways are activated at 6 hr in HCT-15 cells.

claim: HCT-15 cells downregulated genes involved in translation and ribosome biogenesis from 6 hr of exposure.
source: In contrast to BxPC-3 cells, HCT-15 downregulated genes involved in translation and ribosome biogenesis from 6 hr of exposure (Cluster 7, Figure 2D), while intensifying their response to oxidative stress after 12 hr (Cluster 17, Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Supported by clustering and functional enrichment analysis of differential expression data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: HCT-15 cells intensified their response to oxidative stress after 12 hr of treatment.
source: In contrast to BxPC-3 cells, HCT-15 downregulated genes involved in translation and ribosome biogenesis from 6 hr of exposure (Cluster 7, Figure 2D), while intensifying their response to oxidative stress after 12 hr (Cluster 17, Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Supported by clustering and functional enrichment analysis of differential expression data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claim: DNA repair and proteostasis are key mechanisms tuning sensitivity to 3-CePs.
source: In particular, our findings pointed toward DNA repair and proteostasis as key mechanisms tuning sensitivity to the compounds, as further confirmed by inspecting the complete rank of DE genes via gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA, Figure 2—figure supplement 2B; Subramanian et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by gene set enrichment analysis of differential expression data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B, with citation to the GSEA method.

claim: DNA repair was activated in both cell lines early after 6 hr of treatment but with different modulation.
source: Interestingly, DNA repair was activated in both cell lines early after 6 hr of treatment but with a different modulation (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by gene set enrichment analysis of differential expression data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Base-excision repair (BER) was suggested as the preferential pathway of BxPC-3 by gene ontology enrichment.
source: First, base-excision repair (BER) was suggested as the preferential pathway of BxPC-3 by GO enrichment, while HCT-15 relied mostly on nucleotide-excision repair (NER), unleashing a generally stronger activation of the DDR.
evidence: Supported by gene ontology enrichment analysis of differential expression data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: HCT-15 cells relied mostly on nucleotide-excision repair (NER), unleashing a generally stronger activation of the DNA damage response.
source: First, base-excision repair (BER) was suggested as the preferential pathway of BxPC-3 by GO enrichment, while HCT-15 relied mostly on nucleotide-excision repair (NER), unleashing a generally stronger activation of the DDR.
evidence: Supported by gene ontology enrichment analysis of differential expression data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: HCT-15 differential expression genes contributing to the response to the DNA damage stimulus were strongly upregulated already after 6 hr especially in response to B.
source: In detail, HCT-15 DE genes contributing to the response to the DNA damage stimulus were strongly upregulated already after 6 hr especially in response to B, while activated only after 12 hr in BxPC-3 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by expression data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: DNA damage response genes were activated only after 12 hr in BxPC-3 cells.
source: In detail, HCT-15 DE genes contributing to the response to the DNA damage stimulus were strongly upregulated already after 6 hr especially in response to B, while activated only after 12 hr in BxPC-3 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by expression data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: PPP4R2 and RAD51AP1, both involved in the first phases of double-strand breaks repair, were downregulated in BxPC-3 cells at 6 hr.
source: In contrast, genes such as PPP4R2 and RAD51AP1, both involved in the first phases of DSBs repair (Chowdhury et al., 2008; Modesti et al., 2007), were even downregulated in BxPC-3 cells at 6 hr.
evidence: Supported by expression data with citations to prior work on the function of these genes.

claim: Most of the differential expression genes leading the DNA repair enrichment in HCT-15 belonged to nucleotide-excision repair (e.g. GTF2H3 and RBX1) and other recombinational pathways such as homologous repair (e.g. MMS22L and BARD1) and fanconi anemia (e.g. BRIP1 and FANCM).
source: As anticipated, most of the DE genes leading the enrichment in HCT-15 belonged to NER (e.g. GTF2H3 and RBX1) and other recombinational pathways such as homologous repair (HR) (e.g. MMS22L and BARD1) and fanconi anemia (FA) (e.g. BRIP1 and FANCM), all better suited for the efficient repair of bulky lesions and highly toxic DSBs and crosslinks (Cantor et al., 2001; Li and Jin, 2012; Niraj et al., 2019; Piwko et al., 2016; Satoh and Hanawalt, 1996; Westermark et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by gene set enrichment analysis data shown in Figure 3B, with citations to prior work on DNA repair pathways.

claim: Nucleotide-excision repair, homologous repair, and fanconi anemia pathways are better suited for the efficient repair of bulky lesions and highly toxic double-strand breaks and crosslinks.
source: As anticipated, most of the DE genes leading the enrichment in HCT-15 belonged to NER (e.g. GTF2H3 and RBX1) and other recombinational pathways such as homologous repair (HR) (e.g. MMS22L and BARD1) and fanconi anemia (FA) (e.g. BRIP1 and FANCM), all better suited for the efficient repair of bulky lesions and highly toxic DSBs and crosslinks (Cantor et al., 2001; Li and Jin, 2012; Niraj et al., 2019; Piwko et al., 2016; Satoh and Hanawalt, 1996; Westermark et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work on DNA repair pathways.

claim: Differential expression genes in BxPC-3 cells were mostly related to base-excision repair (e.g. APEX1 and UNG) and mismatch repair (e.g. MSH6 and EXO1), which contribute to the repair of smaller lesions and mismatches.
source: On the other hand, DE genes in BxPC-3 cells were mostly related to BER (e.g. APEX1 and UNG) and MMR (mismatch repair) (e.g. MSH6 and EXO1), which contribute to the repair of smaller lesions and mismatches (Fortini et al., 2003; Kunkel and Erie, 2005).
evidence: Supported by gene set enrichment analysis data shown in Figure 3B, with citations to prior work on DNA repair pathways.

claim: Base-excision repair and mismatch repair contribute to the repair of smaller lesions and mismatches.
source: On the other hand, DE genes in BxPC-3 cells were mostly related to BER (e.g. APEX1 and UNG) and MMR (mismatch repair) (e.g. MSH6 and EXO1), which contribute to the repair of smaller lesions and mismatches (Fortini et al., 2003; Kunkel and Erie, 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work on DNA repair pathways.

claim: Proteostasis is a key biological process strictly related to genotoxic stress.
source: In the analysis, proteostasis was identified as a second key biological process strictly related to genotoxic stress (González-Quiroz et al., 2020; Hutt and Balch, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work on the relationship between proteostasis and genotoxic stress.

claim: HCT-15 cells engaged the protein folding and catabolism apparatus in response to 3-CePs, especially to B already at the early time point.
source: HCT-15 cells engaged the protein folding and catabolism apparatus in response to 3-CePs, especially to B already at the early time point (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by gene set enrichment analysis data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Differential expression genes contributing to protein catabolism were upregulated as early as 6 hr of exposure in HCT-15 cells, whereas they were downregulated at the same time point in BxPC-3 and only upregulated after 12 hr.
source: As observed for DNA repair, DE genes contributing to protein catabolism were upregulated as early as 6 hr of exposure in HCT-15 cells, whereas they were downregulated at the same time point in BxPC-3 and only upregulated after 12 hr (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by expression data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: A transcriptional pattern revealed by gene set enrichment analysis at 6 hr of treatment highlighted an intense positive modulation of the PERK-mediated branch of the unfolded protein response specifically in BxPC-3.
source: Interestingly, a transcriptional pattern revealed by GSEA at 6 hr of treatment highlighted an intense positive modulation of the PERK-mediated branch of the unfolded protein response (UPR) specifically in BxPC-3 (Figure 3D and E).
evidence: Supported by gene set enrichment analysis data shown in Figure 3D and E.

claim: ATF4, DDIT3 (CHOP), and PPP1R15A (GADD34) were significantly upregulated after 6 hr of exposure only in BxPC-3 cells.
source: Even more enlightening were the DE genes leading the enrichment: ATF4, DDIT3 (CHOP), and PPP1R15A (GADD34) were significantly upregulated after 6 hr of exposure only in this cell line (Figure 3F).
evidence: Supported by expression data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: ATF4, DDIT3 (CHOP), and PPP1R15A (GADD34) participate in the PERK-mediated unfolded protein response triggering cell death after prolonged ER stress through the aberrant recovery of translation, which induces proteotoxicity.
source: These genes participate in the PERK-mediated UPR triggering cell death after prolonged ER stress through the aberrant recovery of translation, which induces proteotoxicity (Han et al., 2013; Urra et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work on the PERK-mediated UPR pathway.

claim: The PERK-mediated unfolded protein response mechanism would reasonably explain the ribosome biogenesis signature observed in BxPC-3 cells.
source: This mechanism would reasonably explain the ribosome biogenesis signature observed in BxPC-3 cells.
evidence: Based on inference connecting the PERK-mediated UPR pathway to the observed ribosome biogenesis signature.

claim: Recent work reported a particular susceptibility for pancreatic cancer adenocarcinoma to ER stress and protein dyshomeostasis.
source: Consistently, recent work reported a particular susceptibility for pancreatic cancer adenocarcinoma to ER stress and protein dyshomeostasis (Garcia-Carbonero et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work on pancreatic cancer susceptibility to ER stress.

claim: The ability of HCT-15 cells to control proteostasis may depend on the activation of lipid and cholesterol biosynthesis in response to the compounds.
source: Furthermore, the ability of HCT-15 cells to control proteostasis may also depend on the activation of lipid and cholesterol biosynthesis in response to the compounds (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C, D).
evidence: Based on inference from gene set enrichment analysis data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C, D.

claim: Lipid and cholesterol biosynthesis pathways contribute to resolving ER stress through pathways involving the Stearoyl-CoA Desaturase (SCD) enzyme.
source: In fact, among other known pro-survival functions, these pathways contribute to resolving ER stress through pathways involving, e.g., the Stearoyl-CoA Desaturase (SCD) enzyme, for which we detected a significant upregulation of the respective transcript in HCT-15 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D; Romero et al., 2018; Tadros et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by expression data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D, with citations to prior work on lipid metabolism and ER stress.

claim: A significant upregulation of the SCD transcript was detected in HCT-15 cells.
source: In fact, among other known pro-survival functions, these pathways contribute to resolving ER stress through pathways involving, e.g., the Stearoyl-CoA Desaturase (SCD) enzyme, for which we detected a significant upregulation of the respective transcript in HCT-15 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D; Romero et al., 2018; Tadros et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by expression data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Protein homeostasis and DNA damage response imbalances are mechanisms responsible for the high susceptibility of BxPC-3 cells to 3-CePs.
source: Overall, the transcriptome analysis of this in vitro perturbation experiment allowed us to dissect the different responses to 3-CePs in our model cell lines, pointing toward protein homeostasis and DDR imbalances as mechanisms responsible for the high susceptibility of BxPC-3 cells.
evidence: Based on inference from the combined transcriptome analysis results.

claim: Chromatin accessibility was examined in nuclei of BxPC-3 and HCT-15 cells treated with M and B for 6 hr and 12 hr by ATAC-seq.
source: To further characterize them at the epigenetic level, we examined chromatin accessibility in nuclei of BxPC-3 and HCT-15 cells treated with M and B for 6 hr and 12 hr (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A) by ATAC-seq.
evidence: Describes the experimental design for ATAC-seq data collection.

claim: 3-CePs induced evident epigenetic changes in both cell lines, as suggested by principal component analysis and confirmed by the number of differentially accessible regions identified especially in BxPC-3 cells.
source: 3-CePs induced evident epigenetic changes in both cell lines, as suggested by PCA (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B) and confirmed by the number of differentially accessible regions (DARs) identified especially in BxPC-3 cells (p<0.05, Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by PCA and differential accessibility analysis data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B, Figure 4B, and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Condensation of promoters involved in protein catabolism and DNA damage detection was observed in BxPC-3 cells after 6 hr of exposure.
source: In BxPC-3 cells, we observed condensation of promoters involved in protein catabolism and DNA damage detection after 6 hr of exposure (Cluster 1 and 2, Figure 4C), most likely contributing to the transcriptional downregulation of such processes observed at the same time point and in line with the reported improper detection of DNA lesions (Ran et al., 2007; Zhou et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by clustering and functional enrichment analysis of ATAC-seq data shown in Figure 4C, with citations to prior work and inference about biological interpretation.

claim: Relaxation of peaks involved in apoptosis and redox regulation was detected in BxPC-3 cells, in line with evidence from RNA-seq.
source: On the contrary, relaxation of peaks involved in apoptosis and redox regulation was detected, in line with evidence from RNA-seq (Cluster 5, Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by clustering and functional enrichment analysis of ATAC-seq data shown in Figure 4C, consistent with RNA-seq findings.

claim: Relaxation of promoters involved in the DNA damage response as well as protein catabolism was observed in HCT-15 cells.
source: In HCT-15 cells, relaxation of promoters involved in the DDR as well as protein catabolism (Cluster 9 and 10, Figure 4C) was observed, again supporting our observations on transcriptome level.
evidence: Supported by clustering and functional enrichment analysis of ATAC-seq data shown in Figure 4C, consistent with RNA-seq findings.

claim: A cluster of downregulated promoters involved in rRNA transcription was evidenced in HCT-15 cells.
source: Accordingly, we also evidenced a cluster of downregulated promoters involved in rRNA transcription (Cluster 6, Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by clustering and functional enrichment analysis of ATAC-seq data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The regulation of elicited transcriptional pathways was accommodated by changes at the chromatin level.
source: Altogether, these results attested that the regulation of elicited transcriptional pathways was accommodated by changes at the chromatin level, adding new information on the possible mechanisms determining the cellular responses to 3-CePs.
evidence: Based on inference from the combined RNA-seq and ATAC-seq findings.

claim: Pairwise integration identified genes with concordant regulation in RNA- and ATAC-seq upon treatment.
source: As a first level of integration, we identified genes with concordant regulation in RNA- and ATAC-seq upon treatment.
evidence: Describes the pairwise integration approach applied to the data.

claim: The pairwise integration efficiently identified key regulators of previously described processes, highlighting the value of applying multi-omics to gain a higher resolution and robustness in the analysis of drug responses.
source: Overall, the integration efficiently identified key regulators of previously described processes, once more highlighting the value of applying multi-omics to gain a higher resolution and robustness in the analysis of drug responses.
evidence: Based on inference from the results of the pairwise integration analysis.

claim: Coherent upregulation of genes involved in ribosome biogenesis, apoptosis, base-excision repair, and cell cycle regulation was observed at 6 hr of treatment in BxPC-3 cells.
source: As described in Figure 4D for compound M, and similarly for B (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A), we observed coherent upregulation of genes involved in ribosome biogenesis (e.g. RNPS1), apoptosis (e.g. AEN), BER (e.g. APEX1), and cell cycle regulation (e.g. CDC45) at 6 hr of treatment in BxPC-3 cells.
evidence: Supported by pairwise integration analysis data shown in Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Genes regulating the DNA damage response, proteostasis, and redox balance were found to be downregulated consistently in both omic layers at 6 hr in BxPC-3 cells.
source: Meanwhile, at the same conditions, genes regulating the DDR (e.g. MDM2), proteostasis, and redox balance (e.g. GPX1) were found to be downregulated consistently in both omic layers.
evidence: Supported by pairwise integration analysis data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The pairwise integration highlighted double-regulated modulators of protein catabolism, DNA repair, and lipid metabolism in HCT-15 cells.
source: Indeed, the integration highlighted double-regulated modulators of protein catabolism (e.g. PSMA3), DNA repair (e.g. DTL), and lipid metabolism, such as the previously described SCD.
evidence: Supported by pairwise integration analysis data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: HCT-15 cells activated TGF β signaling in response to compound B.
source: Interestingly, these cells also turned out to activate TGF β signaling (e.g. BMPR1A), an important player in cancer drug resistance, in response to B (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A; Brunen et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by pairwise integration analysis data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A, with citation to prior work on TGF β signaling in drug resistance.

claim: TGF β signaling is an important player in cancer drug resistance.
source: Interestingly, these cells also turned out to activate TGF β signaling (e.g. BMPR1A), an important player in cancer drug resistance, in response to B (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A; Brunen et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work on TGF β signaling in drug resistance.

claim: BxPC-3 cells downregulated genes involved in actin remodeling early after 6 hr, a mechanism affecting morphology and function of cancer cells.
source: Furthermore, BxPC-3 cells downregulated, early after 6 hr, genes involved in actin remodeling, a mechanism affecting morphology and function of cancer cells (e.g. CARMIL1) (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A; Caridi et al., 2019; Tafazzoli-Shadpour et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by pairwise integration analysis data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A, with citations to prior work on actin remodeling in cancer cells.

claim: Autophagy is a putative pathway accounting for the enhanced catabolism in HCT-15 cells.
source: Additional insights on double regulation of further processes were evidenced at 12 hr (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B), suggesting for instance autophagy (e.g. CALCOCO2) as a putative pathway accounting for the enhanced catabolism in HCT-15 cells (Chang and Zou, 2020).
evidence: Based on inference from pairwise integration analysis data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2B, with citation to prior work on autophagy.

claim: Pairwise integration of RNA- and ATAC-seq shed light on genes with robust regulation at the transcriptional and chromatin level, adding further details to the previously identified response pathways.
source: Collectively, pairwise integration of RNA- and ATAC-seq shed light on genes with robust regulation at the transcriptional and chromatin level, adding further details to the previously identified response pathways.
evidence: Based on inference from the results of the pairwise integration analysis.

claim: The crosswise integration of transcriptomic and chromatin accessibility data was achieved through an adaptation of the CoCena tool.
source: The crosswise integration of transcriptomic and chromatin accessibility data was achieved through an adaptation of the CoCena (construction of co-expression network analysis - automated) tool which inspects the pattern of regulation of genes across conditions in a single transcriptome dataset.
evidence: Describes the methodological approach for crosswise integration.

claim: The vertical, inter-omic integration (vCoCena) was applied to construct the final network consolidating the information from transcriptome and chromatin accessibility.
source: At this point, the vertical, inter-omic integration (vCoCena) was applied to construct the final network consolidating the information from transcriptome and chromatin accessibility (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D, see Methods for details).
evidence: Describes the methodological approach for crosswise integration.

claim: The orchid and light blue clusters suggested macroautophagy as a putative pathway accounting for the enhanced catabolism observed in HCT-15 cells.
source: Some modules validated the information obtained through previous analyses (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E): both the orchid and light blue clusters suggested macroautophagy as a putative pathway accounting for the enhanced catabolism observed in HCT-15 cells (Chang and Zou, 2020).
evidence: Supported by crosswise integration analysis data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1E, with citation to prior work on autophagy.

claim: The maroon module, upregulated after 6 hr in BxPC-3, contains genes involved in ribosome biogenesis, base-excision repair, and apoptosis.
source: Another mostly RNA-seq-based module validating our previous approach was the maroon module, upregulated after 6 hr in BxPC-3, containing genes involved in ribosome biogenesis, BER, and apoptosis.
evidence: Supported by crosswise integration analysis data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1E.

claim: The dark green and dark gray ATAC modules, downregulated in BxPC-3 cells, include genes modulating redox metabolism and ER stress.
source: Furthermore, the dark green and dark gray ATAC modules, downregulated in BxPC-3 cells, include genes modulating redox metabolism and ER stress.
evidence: Supported by crosswise integration analysis data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1E.

claim: The dark orange RNA module includes genes downregulated in HCT-15 cells at 6 hr but upregulated in BxPC-3 responding to M, belonging to the Wnt signaling pathway.
source: Other modules offered instead a new perspective on the reactions of the two cell lines: the dark orange RNA module includes genes downregulated in HCT-15 cells at 6 hr but upregulated in BxPC-3 responding to M. Interestingly, these hits belong to the Wnt signaling pathway, well-known for regulating ribosome biogenesis and cell growth, adding further information on our initial findings.
evidence: Supported by crosswise integration analysis data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1E, with inference about biological interpretation.

claim: The Wnt signaling pathway is well-known for regulating ribosome biogenesis and cell growth.
source: Other modules offered instead a new perspective on the reactions of the two cell lines: the dark orange RNA module includes genes downregulated in HCT-15 cells at 6 hr but upregulated in BxPC-3 responding to M. Interestingly, these hits belong to the Wnt signaling pathway, well-known for regulating ribosome biogenesis and cell growth, adding further information on our initial findings.
evidence: Draws from established scientific knowledge about the Wnt signaling pathway.

claim: The indian red module, upregulated in HCT-15 cells, points toward the tumorigenic JAK-STAT as an additional pathway modulating drug resistance.
source: In addition, the indian red module, upregulated in HCT-15 cells, points toward the tumorigenic JAK-STAT as an additional pathway modulating drug resistance (Brooks and Putoczki, 2020).
evidence: Supported by crosswise integration analysis data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1E, with citation to prior work on JAK-STAT signaling in drug resistance.

claim: The steelblue module's 174 genes are positively modulated in HCT-15 cells especially after 6 hr of treatment.
source: The crosswise integration also identified additional regulation, exemplified by the steelblue module. As approximated by the associated GFCs pattern, its 174 genes are positively modulated in HCT-15 cells especially after 6 hr of treatment (Figure 5D).
evidence: Supported by crosswise integration analysis data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Functional enrichment of the steelblue module identified hits from both RNA- and ATAC-seq involved in the tumorigenic epithelial-mesenchymal transition.
source: Interestingly, functional enrichment identified hits both from RNA- and ATAC-seq involved in the tumorigenic epithelial-mesenchymal transition (Figure 5E), a mechanism regulating morphology and invasiveness of cancer cells (e.g. KBTBD8, Figure 5—figure supplement 1F, from the RNA-seq layer) (Brabletz et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by functional enrichment analysis of the steelblue module shown in Figure 5E, with citation to prior work on EMT.

claim: Epithelial-mesenchymal transition is a mechanism regulating morphology and invasiveness of cancer cells.
source: Interestingly, functional enrichment identified hits both from RNA- and ATAC-seq involved in the tumorigenic epithelial-mesenchymal transition (Figure 5E), a mechanism regulating morphology and invasiveness of cancer cells (e.g. KBTBD8, Figure 5—figure supplement 1F, from the RNA-seq layer) (Brabletz et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work on EMT.

claim: The steelblue module included genes of recombinational DNA repair belonging to both omic layers.
source: In addition, the module included genes of recombinational DNA repair belonging to both omic layers, which is in line with our initial findings (e.g. AUNIP; Figure 5E and Figure 5—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Supported by functional enrichment analysis of the steelblue module shown in Figure 5E and Figure 5—figure supplement 1F.

claim: The crosswise integration of RNA- and ATAC-seq data allowed an efficient combination of the functional information from the two omics layers.
source: Overall, the crosswise integration of RNA- and ATAC-seq data allowed an efficient combination of the functional information from the two omics layers.
evidence: Based on inference from the results of the crosswise integration analysis.

claim: The whole integration added further biology to what was identified when analyzing transcriptional and chromatin landscape regulation individually.
source: Clearly, the whole integration added further biology to what we had identified when analyzing transcriptional and chromatin landscape regulation individually.
evidence: Based on inference from the results of the crosswise integration analysis.

claim: Gene ontology enrichment on the signature genes identified protein synthesis, folding and catabolism, lipid metabolism, matrix organization, and actin remodeling among the most significant biological functions.
source: GO enrichment on these genes identified protein synthesis, folding and catabolism, lipid metabolism, matrix organization, and actin remodeling among the most significant biological functions (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by gene ontology enrichment analysis of the signature genes shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: BNIP3, SCD, and SLFN11 are interesting genes in the up signature.
source: Some interesting genes in the up signature were BNIP3, proapoptotic, SCD, the already discussed regulator of lipid metabolism and SLFN11, involved in DDR and known response biomarker (Zoppoli et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by the signature composition with citation to prior work on SLFN11.

claim: SLFN11 is involved in DNA damage response and is a known response biomarker.
source: Some interesting genes in the up signature were BNIP3, proapoptotic, SCD, the already discussed regulator of lipid metabolism and SLFN11, involved in DDR and known response biomarker (Zoppoli et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work on SLFN11.

claim: YOD1, HERPUD1, HSPA5, ERCC6, and AUNIP are genes composing the down signature.
source: Among those composing the down signature, we identified YOD1, HERPUD1, and HSPA5, involved in protein homeostasis and ER stress, but also ERCC6 and AUNIP of the DDR (Figure 6B; Ernst et al., 2009; Lou et al., 2017; Pascucci et al., 2018; Schulze et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by the signature composition with citations to prior work on these genes.

claim: The perturbation-informed signature demonstrated a strong predictive capacity as attested by the high positive correlation between viability decrease and predicted sensitivity score (Pearson's R: 0.834, p: 0.0398).
source: As shown in Figure 6C, our perturbation-informed signature demonstrated a strong predictive capacity as attested by the high positive correlation between viability decrease and predicted sensitivity score (Pearson's R: 0.834, p: 0.0398; Figure 6C).
evidence: Supported by experimental validation data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The perturbation-informed signature outperformed a random signature containing the same number of genes (R: −0.023, p: 0.97).
source: This signature outperformed a random one containing the same number of genes (R: −0.023, p: 0.97, Figure 6—figure supplement 1D) and also a signature of equal size composed by the top up- and down-regulated genes between the two cell lines (R: 0.33, p: 0.52, Figure 6—figure supplement 1E, gene list available in Supplementary file 7).
evidence: Supported by experimental validation data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The perturbation-informed signature outperformed a signature of equal size composed by the top up- and down-regulated genes between the two cell lines (R: 0.33, p: 0.52).
source: This signature outperformed a random one containing the same number of genes (R: −0.023, p: 0.97, Figure 6—figure supplement 1D) and also a signature of equal size composed by the top up- and down-regulated genes between the two cell lines (R: 0.33, p: 0.52, Figure 6—figure supplement 1E, gene list available in Supplementary file 7).
evidence: Supported by experimental validation data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1E.

claim: The crosswise integration approach resulted in a perturbation-informed signature capable of predicting drug sensitivity in a wide range of untreated tumor cell lines commonly used in cancer research.
source: Collectively, our crosswise integration approach resulted in a perturbation-informed signature capable of predicting drug sensitivity in a wide range of untreated tumor cell lines commonly used in cancer research.
evidence: Based on inference from the validation results of the signature.

claim: GSVA examination of TCGA tumor samples unveiled which cancer types were predicted as generally more susceptible (i.e. kidney renal clear cell carcinoma [KIRC], PAAD, glioblastoma multiforme [GBM], and kidney renal papillary cell carcinoma [KIRP]) or less sensitive (i.e. rectum adenocarcinoma, colon adenocarcinoma [COAD], uterine corpus endometrial carcinoma, cervical squamous cell carcinoma and endocervical adenocarcinoma) to M.
source: By applying GSVA, we examined the relative distribution of samples from different tumor types based on the calculated sensitivity score, unveiling which cancer types were predicted as generally more susceptible (i.e. kidney renal clear cell carcinoma [KIRC], PAAD, glioblastoma multiforme [GBM], and kidney renal papillary cell carcinoma [KIRP]) or less sensitive (i.e. rectum adenocarcinoma, colon adenocarcinoma [COAD], uterine corpus endometrial carcinoma, cervical squamous cell carcinoma and endocervical adenocarcinoma) to M, providing a framework for further in vivo development of this compound (Figure 6D).
evidence: Supported by GSVA analysis of TCGA data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The predicted tumor type with the highest sensitivity to M turned out to be kidney renal clear cell carcinoma (KIRC).
source: Interestingly, the predicted tumor type with the highest sensitivity turned out to be KIRC, demonstrating that the designed signature was not driven by the original cell type of the cell lines used for its extrapolation and could go beyond the original cancer type.
evidence: Supported by GSVA analysis of TCGA data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The designed signature was not driven by the original cell type of the cell lines used for its extrapolation and could go beyond the original cancer type.
source: Interestingly, the predicted tumor type with the highest sensitivity turned out to be KIRC, demonstrating that the designed signature was not driven by the original cell type of the cell lines used for its extrapolation and could go beyond the original cancer type.
evidence: Based on inference from the observation that KIRC, not the original cell type, was predicted as most sensitive.

claim: Intra-tumor variability resulted in a continuous distribution of samples scores within each cancer group, confirming the importance of clinically translating such predictions beyond the tumor type to better address patient-specific therapeutic needs.
source: Interestingly, intra-tumor variability resulted in a continuous distribution of samples scores within each cancer group, confirming the importance of clinically translating such predictions beyond the tumor type to better address patient-specific therapeutic needs.
evidence: Based on inference from the observed distribution of sensitivity scores within tumor types.

claim: A LASSO regression model was introduced to predict the sensitivity of tumor samples in the external reference dataset.
source: To enlarge the accessibility and clinical translatability of our framework, we finally introduced a LASSO regression model to predict the sensitivity of tumor samples in the external reference dataset (Figure 6E).
evidence: Describes the methodological approach for machine learning-based prediction.

claim: The LASSO regression model efficiently predicted drug sensitivity within the test samples (R: 0.97, RMSE: 0.069).
source: In detail, TCGA samples were labeled according to the calculated continuous sensitivity scores. Next, the model was trained on 80% of the data and tested on the remaining 20%, which efficiently predicted drug sensitivity within the test samples (R: 0.97, RMSE: 0.069) (Figure 6F).
evidence: Supported by machine learning model performance data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: The predictive capacity of the LASSO model was maintained even when excluding from the transcriptomes all the signature genes used to define the sensitivity score label of the samples (R: 0.97, RMSE: 0.072).
source: Notably, such predictive capacity was maintained even when excluding from the transcriptomes all the signature genes used to define the sensitivity score label of the samples, suggesting the biological robustness of the predictive system (R: 0.97, RMSE: 0.072; Figure 6—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Supported by machine learning model performance data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1F.

claim: While the signature itself was good enough to rank samples based on experimental biological evidence, the model went beyond the initial signature by relying on additional predictive features previously not identified.
source: In fact, while the signature itself was good enough to rank samples based on experimental biological evidence, the model went beyond the initial signature by relying on additional predictive features previously not identified.
evidence: Based on inference from the observation that the model performs well even without the signature genes.

claim: The classifier performed well also on separate cancer types, demonstrating its capacity to address intra-tumor type heterogeneity.
source: Moreover, the classifier performed well also on separate cancer types, demonstrating its capacity to address intra-tumor type heterogeneity (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Supported by machine learning model performance data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The same analysis pipeline was applied to the prediction of cancer cell lines' sensitivity to cisplatin.
source: As a last validation step to confirm the versatility of our approach, we applied the pipeline to the prediction of cancer cell lines' sensitivity to cisplatin, a thoroughly reported broad-acting chemotherapeutic introduced as a DNA damaging agent (Kelland, 2007).
evidence: Describes the application of the pipeline to cisplatin, with citation to prior work on cisplatin.

claim: Cisplatin is a thoroughly reported broad-acting chemotherapeutic introduced as a DNA damaging agent.
source: As a last validation step to confirm the versatility of our approach, we applied the pipeline to the prediction of cancer cell lines' sensitivity to cisplatin, a thoroughly reported broad-acting chemotherapeutic introduced as a DNA damaging agent (Kelland, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work on cisplatin.

claim: Jurkat and BxPC-3 cells were selected as high- and low-sensitive cancer cell lines to cisplatin based on the IC50s reported in the Genomics of Drug Sensitivity in Cancer database (Jurkat: 3 µM, BxPC-3: 55 µM).
source: First, we selected Jurkat and BxPC-3 cells as high- and low-sensitive cancer cell lines based on the IC50s reported in the Genomics of Drug Sensitivity in Cancer database (Jurkat: 3 µM, BxPC-3: 55 µM) (Yang et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to the Genomics of Drug Sensitivity in Cancer database.

claim: The cisplatin signature predicted sensitivity to this reference drug with high accuracy, showing a strong anticorrelation between predicted sensitivity score and actual IC50 (Pearson's R: −0.76, p: 0.007).
source: Results confirmed the applicability of our approach, which predicted sensitivity to this reference drug with high accuracy, showing a strong anticorrelation between predicted sensitivity score and actual IC50 (Pearsons's R: −0.76, p: 0.007, Figure 6G).
evidence: Supported by experimental validation data shown in Figure 6G.

claim: The prediction on TCGA tumor transcriptomes highlighted testicular germ cell tumor (TGCT) as the most sensitive cancer type to cisplatin.
source: Even more promising, despite the fact that our model was not trained on data derived from testicular cancer, the prediction on TCGA tumor transcriptomes highlighted testicular germ cell tumor TGCT as the most sensitive cancer type (Figure 6H), a finding that is clinically confirmed being testicular cancer efficiently treated with cisplatin since decades (Kelland, 2007).
evidence: Supported by GSVA analysis of TCGA data shown in Figure 6H.

claim: Testicular cancer is efficiently treated with cisplatin since decades.
source: Even more promising, despite the fact that our model was not trained on data derived from testicular cancer, the prediction on TCGA tumor transcriptomes highlighted testicular germ cell tumor TGCT as the most sensitive cancer type (Figure 6H), a finding that is clinically confirmed being testicular cancer efficiently treated with cisplatin since decades (Kelland, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work on cisplatin treatment of testicular cancer.

claim: The integrated RNA- and ATAC-seq information was employed to assemble an accurate and clinically-accessible predictive strategy capable of orienting drug development and supporting medical practice in the context of precision oncology.
source: Overall, we demonstrated how to further employ the integrated RNA- and ATAC-seq information to assemble an accurate and clinically-accessible predictive strategy capable of orienting drug development and supporting medical practice in the context of precision oncology.
evidence: Based on inference from the combined results of the signature construction and validation.

claim: The multi-omics pipeline not only allowed to identify potentially more susceptible target tumor types for further development of test compounds, but also offered a complete predictive framework to support precision oncology in a clinical setting.
source: Overall, the proposed pipeline not only allowed to identify potentially more susceptible target tumor types for further development of test compounds, but also offered a complete predictive framework to support precision oncology in a clinical setting.
evidence: Based on inference from the combined results of the study.

claim: The modularity of the framework allows, with only minimal adjustment, its application to other omic technologies or experimental designs.
source: Nevertheless, the modularity of our framework allows, with only minimal adjustment, its application to other omic technologies or experimental designs.
evidence: Based on speculation about the generalizability of the approach.

claim: The pipeline showed to be versatile, being applicable to other drugs and, as a consequence, generalizable to other diseases and target cell populations.
source: The pipeline showed to be versatile, being applicable to other drugs and, as a consequence, generalizable to other diseases and target cell populations.
evidence: Based on inference from the successful application to both 3-CePs and cisplatin.

claim: The vCoCena integration is instrumental for both the biological interpretation of the data and the definition of the perturbation-informed signature.
source: Indeed, the vCoCena integration, which is instrumental for both the biological interpretation of the data and the definition of the perturbation-informed signature, is agnostic of the type of data used as soon as this is reduced to a network of co-regulation.
evidence: Based on inference from the design and application of the vCoCena method.

claim: The vCoCena integration is agnostic of the type of data used as soon as this is reduced to a network of co-regulation.
source: Indeed, the vCoCena integration, which is instrumental for both the biological interpretation of the data and the definition of the perturbation-informed signature, is agnostic of the type of data used as soon as this is reduced to a network of co-regulation.
evidence: Based on the design of the vCoCena method.

claim: The workflow provides a human-readable toolbox to interrogate pharmacological questions in both preclinical and clinical settings.
source: In conclusion, we present a complete end-to-end workflow to implement the use of multi-omics in drug development, providing a human-readable toolbox to interrogate pharmacological questions in both preclinical and clinical settings.
evidence: Based on inference from the design and application of the workflow.

claim: The workflow is a broadly applicable resource to assist researchers in different steps of the drug discovery and development process.
source: Given its versatility, we envision our workflow to be a broadly applicable resource to assist researchers in different steps of the drug discovery and development process.
evidence: Based on speculation about the future applicability of the workflow.
